title: Reverse a Doubly Linked List
directAnswer: For each node, swap its next and prev pointers, then move forward along the *old* next — which you must read before the swap, because the swap overwrites it. The last node you process becomes the new head. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space, no new nodes.

remember.pattern: Swap next/prev per node, walk along the saved old-next, return the last node as head
remember.formula:
cur = head
newHead = head
while cur:
    nxt = cur.next        # read before swapping
    cur.next = cur.prev
    cur.prev = nxt
    newHead = cur
    cur = nxt
return newHead
rules: Save `cur.next` into a temp **before** swapping — the swap destroys it and you lose your way forward (the lost-next trap).
Swap **both** pointers per node: `next ↔ prev`. Touching only one leaves the list half-rewired and corrupt.
The new head is the **last** node you process (the old tail), not `head` — return it.
Advance using the saved old-next, never `cur.next` after the swap (which now points backward).
An empty or single-node list reverses to itself — the loop handles both without special branches.
whenToUse: Reverse a list that has both next and prev links (doubly linked)
You need O(1) extra space and can mutate the existing nodes
Any 'flip the direction of traversal' task on a bidirectional structure
Preparing a DLL for backward iteration or LRU-style reordering
antiSignals: The list is singly linked → there is no prev to swap; use the three-pointer prev/cur/next reversal
You must keep the original order intact → copy or iterate backward instead of mutating
Only a backward *view* is needed, not a true reversal → just walk prev pointers from the tail
Nodes are immutable → you cannot swap fields; rebuild instead
remember.takeaway: Reversing a DLL is just 'swap next and prev on every node'. The only subtlety is reading the old next before the swap clobbers it, and remembering the new head is the old tail. Master this and reverse-a-sublist and rotate on a DLL follow directly.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize a DLL reversal is a per-node pointer swap rather than a rebuild, and whether you correctly save the forward pointer before overwriting it and return the old tail as the new head.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Advancing via cur.next after swapping (which now points backward, causing an infinite loop or early exit), or returning the original head instead of the last processed node.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the two invariants: swap both pointers per node, and capture old-next first. Note the new head is the old tail, and that empty/single-node lists fall out of the loop for free — no special cases.

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a **doubly linked list**, where each node has a `val`, a `next` pointer, and a `prev` pointer.

Reverse the list in place by re-pointing each node's links, and return *the head of the reversed list*.

Do not allocate new nodes — rewire the existing ones.
constraints: Each node has both next and prev pointers (prev of head is null, next of tail is null)
Must run in O(1) extra space
understanding: In a doubly linked list every node points both forward (next) and backward (prev). Reversing means every node that used to point forward should now point backward and vice versa — so for each node we simply swap its next and prev. The old tail becomes the new head.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is this a singly or doubly linked list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Doubly — every node has both next and prev. That's what lets us reverse by swapping the two pointers per node instead of the three-pointer dance a singly linked list needs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I mutate the existing nodes or must I build a new list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Mutate in place. Swapping pointers gives O(1) extra space; rebuilding would waste O(n) memory.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return for an empty or single-node list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The same head. An empty list reverses to empty; a single node reverses to itself. Both fall out of the loop naturally.

clarifyingQuestions.question: After reversal, what should prev of the new head and next of the new tail be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The new head's prev is null and the new tail's next is null — the swaps produce exactly that, since the old head's next was null becomes the old head's prev.

examples.explanation: Each node swaps next/prev; node 3 (old tail) becomes the new head, node 1 (old head) becomes the new tail.
Single node: swapping its null next and null prev leaves it unchanged; it's its own head.
head is null, the loop never runs, and we return null.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Iterative pointer-swap is the O(1)-space default; recursion is elegant but costs O(n) stack.

approaches.name: Iterative — Swap next/prev on Each Node (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. The per-node swap is the idiom interviewers want for DLL reversal, and it's O(1) space.
hints: In a doubly linked list each node already knows the node before and after it. If you flipped the meaning of those two fields on every node, which direction would the list read in?
Swapping cur.next and cur.prev destroys the forward link you need to keep walking. What must you grab before the swap?
After the loop ends, cur is null — so which node did you last touch, and what role does it now play in the reversed list?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly one visit per node, each doing O(1) pointer swaps → O(n) time. Only a couple of temp pointers are used → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We walk the list once and, at every node, exchange its `next` and `prev` so the node now points the opposite way.

**Why a single swap per node suffices.** In a DLL, 'reversed' means: the node that was your successor should become your predecessor and vice versa. That is literally swapping the two pointer fields. There's no need to rebuild links across nodes — each node fixes its own two pointers, and because every node does it, the whole chain flips consistently.

**Save the old next first — the lost-next trap.** The catch is that we navigate forward using `cur.next`, but the swap *overwrites* `cur.next` with the old `prev`. So before swapping we copy `cur.next` into a temp `nxt`. After swapping, `cur.next` points backward (useless for moving forward), so we advance with `cur = nxt`. Skip the save and you either loop forever (following the now-backward pointer) or stop one node in.

**Why the new head is the old tail.** We keep updating `newHead = cur` on every iteration. The loop runs until `cur` becomes null, which happens right after we process the old tail. So the last node we touched — the old tail — is the node we return. Its old `next` was null, and after the swap that null lands in its `prev`, exactly the correct prev-of-head.

**Why empty and single-node need no special case.** If `head` is null the loop body never runs and `newHead` stays null. For one node, `nxt` is null, we swap its two null-ish pointers, set `newHead = cur`, then `cur = null` ends the loop — the node is returned unchanged.
approaches.insight: The whole trick is recognizing that DLL reversal decomposes into n independent per-node swaps. The only cross-node concern is preserving the forward pointer before the swap eats it — the same 'stash the next pointer' reflex from every in-place list rewrite.

dryRun.intro: cur walks forward along the SAVED old-next. Each node swaps next/prev; newHead tracks the last node touched.

code.python:
class DoublyLinkedListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None, prev=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
        self.prev = prev

def reverse(self, head: DoublyLinkedListNode) -> DoublyLinkedListNode:
    cur = head
    new_head = head
    while cur is not None:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = cur.prev
        cur.prev = nxt
        new_head = cur
        cur = nxt
    return new_head

java.explanation: Capture the forward pointer BEFORE the swap clobbers it — the lost-next trap.
First half of the swap: the old predecessor becomes the new successor.
Second half: the saved old successor becomes the new predecessor.
Track the last node touched — the old tail will be the final value, our new head.
Advance using the saved old-next, NOT cur.next (which now points backward).

python.explanation: Save the old forward link before overwriting it.
Saved old next becomes new prev — both pointers flipped.
Remember this node; the last one set is the old tail = new head.
Step forward along the saved old-next pointer.

pitfalls: Advancing with cur = cur.next after the swap — that pointer now goes backward, causing an infinite loop or premature stop.
Swapping only next (or only prev) — leaves the list inconsistent and corrupt.
Returning the original head instead of the last node (old tail).
Forgetting to save old-next before swapping — the lost-next trap that strands the rest of the list.

edgeCases.behavior: head is null; loop never runs; newHead stays null → returns null.
nxt = null, swap leaves the single node's pointers null, newHead = node, cur = null → returns the same node.

approaches.name: Recursive — Swap at the Node, Recurse on the Old Next
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as a tidy alternative; flag the O(n) recursion stack versus the iterative O(1) space.
hints: If you swap the current node's next/prev, what's left to reverse, and where does the new head come from?
Save the old next before swapping, then recurse on that saved node.
The base case is reaching null or the old tail — the node with no old-next is the new head that bubbles back up.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One call per node → O(n) calls, each O(1) work → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals the node count → O(n) stack space.
approaches.explanation:
We do the same per-node swap, but let the call stack drive the walk.

**Base case identifies the new head.** If `head` is null, return null. Otherwise, after we swap the current node's pointers, if the saved old-next is null this node is the old tail — the new head — and we return it up the chain.

**Swap, then recurse on the saved old-next.** Read `nxt = head.next` first (the lost-next trap applies here too), swap `head.next` and `head.prev`, then recurse on `nxt`. The recursive call reverses the remainder and returns the eventual new head, which every level simply passes upward unchanged — the actual relinking already happened via the local swap.

**Why iterative is the safer lead.** The recursion mirrors the loop exactly but adds a stack frame per node. With n up to 10⁴ that risks a deep stack; the iterative O(1)-space version has no such limit. Same time, more space — present iterative first.
approaches.insight: Recursion turns the explicit `newHead` bookkeeping into a return value: the base case (old tail) hands the new head back up, and each frame just forwards it. The per-node swap is identical to the loop — only the driver changes.

dryRun.intro: Each call swaps its node, then recurses on the saved old-next; the base case returns the new head up the chain.

steps.action: nxt=null; swap 3; nxt is null → return 3

java.explanation: Empty list base case — nothing to reverse.
Save old-next before the swap destroys it.
Swap this node's two pointers, flipping its direction.
No old-next means this is the old tail = new head; return it.
Recurse on the saved old-next and pass the eventual new head straight up.

python.explanation: Flip next to point at the old predecessor.
Old tail reached — this node is the new head.
Reverse the rest; the new head propagates up unchanged.

pitfalls: Swapping after reading head.next incorrectly — always save old-next first.
Recursing on head.next after the swap — it now points backward; recurse on the saved nxt.
Deep recursion on long lists risks stack overflow where the iterative version is safe.

commonMistakes: Advancing via cur.next after swapping, when that field now points backward.
Swapping only one of the two pointers, leaving the list inconsistent.
Returning the original head rather than the old tail (the new head).
Not saving the old-next before the swap, stranding the rest of the list.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Walking forward with the post-swap next pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After the swap, cur.next holds the old prev — it points backward. Using it to advance either revisits earlier nodes forever or exits after one step. You must move along the saved old-next.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Swapping only one pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Reversal requires both fields to flip. Setting next but not prev (or vice versa) leaves nodes whose forward and backward links disagree, corrupting any later traversal in either direction.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
nxt = cur.next
cur.next = cur.prev
# forgot: cur.prev = nxt
cur = nxt
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
nxt = cur.next
cur.next = cur.prev
cur.prev = nxt
cur = nxt

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the original head
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After reversal the original head is the new tail. Returning it hands back a node whose next is null, so the caller sees a one-node list. The new head is the last node processed (old tail).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while cur is not None:
    # ... swap ...
    cur = nxt
return head   # head is now the tail!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
new_head = head
while cur is not None:
    # ... swap ...
    new_head = cur
    cur = nxt
return new_head
